questions.question: A test asserts that a retry loop took between 1.5 and 4 seconds of wall-clock time. It passes locally and fails on the build agent about one run in twenty. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The build agent's JVM has a smaller default heap, so garbage collection runs more often and slows the loop
The build agent runs an older Java version whose timers are coarser and less accurate than the laptop's
The test samples wall-clock time and random jitter, so its outcome is a distribution, not a verdict
The retry loop has a data race that only manifests on the agent's multi-core virtual machine
questions.explanation: Elapsed time and unseeded jitter are inputs the test did not choose; a GC pause or a run of small jitter draws moves the result outside the window. Injecting a FakeClock and a SeededRandom turns the sample into a deterministic assertion. A race condition is possible but would not explain why the window-based assertion is the thing that fails.

questions.question: Why does the Java track carry a hand-written check() harness in every MainTest.java instead of using JUnit?
options: JUnit cannot assert on thrown exceptions, which the money and ledger lessons depend on heavily
The course is standard-library only and the JDK ships no test runner, so the harness lives in the file
JUnit needs a build tool such as Maven or Gradle, and javac alone cannot process its annotations
The hand-written harness starts faster than JUnit, which matters for the benchmarking lesson's timings
questions.explanation: Rule 3 forbids libraries, and unlike Python (unittest) and Go (testing) the JDK has no built-in runner, so each lesson's test file contains its own check, checkEquals, and checkThrows plus a main that exits 1. JUnit does assert on exceptions and does not need a build tool; those are not the reasons. Speed is irrelevant at this scale.

questions.question: FakeClock.advanceTo(1_999) is called on a clock currently at 2_000. What happens, and why is the rule enforced on a fake?
options: It is rejected, because code under test may compute now minus last and a rewind would test an impossible negative duration
The clock moves to 1_999 so that tests can simulate NTP step corrections and VM migrations realistically
It is silently ignored and the clock stays at 2_000, so that tests never fail because of clock setup mistakes
The clock resets to its construction value and discards every advance made since, so the test restarts cleanly
questions.explanation: The invariant is monotonicity: a rejected move leaves the clock at 2_000 and raises. Allowing a rewind would let a test exercise impossible states such as negative elapsed time. Real clocks can step backwards, but that is modelled explicitly in Phase 5 with a monotonic clock, not by letting the ordinary fake drift. Silently ignoring the call would hide a test bug.

questions.question: SeededRandom is implemented as SplitMix64 rather than wrapping java.util.Random, random.Random, and math/rand. What does this buy the course?
options: Cryptographic strength, so the same type can be reused to generate idempotency keys and nonces in Phase 12
A much longer period than any of the three standard-library generators, so long simulations never repeat
The same sequence for the same seed in all three languages, so 'with seed 7 the third message is lost' holds everywhere
Faster generation than the Mersenne Twister, whose 2.5 KB state is expensive to keep in cache during simulation
questions.explanation: The three standard-library generators are different algorithms and produce unrelated sequences from the same seed. Ten lines of 64-bit wrapping arithmetic give identical output everywhere, which the published test vector for seed 1234567 confirms. SplitMix64 is explicitly not cryptographic: its whole state is recoverable from one output, and its 2^64 period is shorter than Mersenne Twister's.

questions.question: In the Go test file, mustEqual calls t.Helper() before comparing. What changes if that line is removed?
options: The file stops compiling, because Go requires any function that takes *testing.T to call t.Helper() first
A failure is reported at the line inside mustEqual rather than at the caller, hiding which table row produced it
The helper can no longer be called from inside a t.Run subtest, because subtests get their own *testing.T
t.Errorf behaves like t.Fatalf, so the first mismatch aborts the whole test instead of recording and continuing
questions.explanation: t.Helper() marks the function so the runner skips its frame when attributing a failure, so the report names the caller's line. Without it every failure from the table-driven test points at the same line in the helper. It has no effect on compilation, on subtests, or on whether the test continues after a mismatch.

questions.question: The thread test advances a shared FakeClock from eight workers and asserts the total. Why is `go test -race` the better check than the assertion alone?
options: The race detector proves the mutex is unnecessary by showing that the goroutines never access `now` at the same time
The assertion cannot execute under -race, because the detector refuses to run tests that share a variable between goroutines
The race detector forces goroutines to run strictly one after another, so the total is always exact and the test cannot flake
Without the mutex the total is often still correct by chance, but the detector reports the unsynchronised accesses every run
questions.explanation: A lost update needs an unlucky interleaving, so the plain assertion can pass many times with the bug present. The detector instruments every access and reports two unsynchronised accesses to `now` deterministically, with both stack traces. It does not serialise goroutines and it does not forbid shared state; it watches how shared state is accessed.
